list.listitem: In patients suspected of having dementia with vascular risk factors or atherosclerotic disease, neuroimaging showing evidence of brain infarction is highly suggestive of multi-infarct dementia (MID). C
Cholinesterase inhibitors offer modest benefit for cognitive function and activities of daily living (ADLs) in patients with MID but may cause significant side effects. B
Possibly effective nonpharmacologic measures include massage therapy, cognitive training, light therapy, aerobic exercise, graded assistance, and caregiver intervention. B
Control of vascular risk factors such as hypertension and hyperlipidemia have not been demonstrated to improve cognitive function and ADLs in patients with MID. C
MID is irreversible, and a stepwise decline in cognitive and behavioral function is expected with a mean survival after diagnosis of about 4 to 5 years. B

background.definition: Multi-infarct dementia (MID), also called vascular dementia, is an acquired deterioration in memory and cognitive abilities associated with cerebrovascular disease that impairs successful performance of ADLs, and is usually associated with focal neurological deficits and discrete episodes of sudden cognitive deterioration.

list.listitem: It is estimated that dementia affects up to 30% of Americans older than 85 years, and MID is suggested in 8% to 15% of patients with cognitive impairment.
Prevalence of MID may reach 25% to 35% of elderly Asian patients with dementia.
Estimated health care cost is $10 billion to $20 billion annually.

Patients with a nonfocal transient ischemic attack (sudden decreased consciousness, confusion, unsteadiness, neurologic symptoms, resolving within 24 hours) are at increased risk of dementia, especially vascular dementia (13% vs 10%).
A meta-analysis of six longitudinal studies found that patients with hypertension were at increased risk of developing MID (OR 1.6; CI 1.3-2.0).
MID is thought to be caused by cerebrovascular disease that leads to infarction of brain tissue, usually as separate events.
These episodes of infarction lead to neurologic deficits, memory loss, loss of executive function, and behavioral disturbances.
There is insufficient evidence to support routine screening for dementia in patients who do not otherwise exhibit evidence of cognitive impairment.B

Control of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and aspirin therapy decrease the incidence of cerebrovascular accident (CVA), which is the presumed etiology of MID, but no rigorous studies have demonstrated that this specifically prevents MID.C
No currently available medications prevent cognitive decline, cognitive impairment, or dementia. B
There is good evidence that giving statins to patients at risk for vascular dementia does not reduce the risk of vascular dementia. A
Smokers are at increased risk of MID compared to patients who have never smoked. B
Suspect MID in patients with dementia who have vascular risk factors, atherosclerotic disease, or focal neurologic deficits. C
If MID is suspected, obtain a brain MRI with and without contrast. C
Neuroimaging showing evidence of infarction or white matter hyperintensities in a patient with dementia is highly suggestive of MID. C

Differential.Differential_Features: More progressive, no specific neuroimaging or neurological exam findings
Associated with Parkinsonism and more dramatic cognitive fluctuations
Begins with and more characterized by marked behavioral disturbances

list.listitem: According to Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (Third Edition Revised), stepwise development of multiple cognitive deficits is manifested by memory impairment and by aphasia, apraxia, agnosia, and/or disturbance in executive function not associated with delirium.
Deficits cause significant decline in overall function.
Focal neurological signs and/or laboratory/radiologic evidence suggesting cerebrovascular disease are present.
A memory complaint coupled with global cognitive impairment should prompt suspicion of dementia.
A stepwise decline in memory and executive function associated with a history of cerebrovascular disease is suggestive of MID.
Physical examination often yields focal neurological findings such as Babinski's sign, pseudobulbar palsy, gait abnormalities, exaggeration of deep tendon reflexes, or extremity weakness.
MRI of the brain with and without contrast usually shows evidence of infarction, helps distinguish from other forms of dementia, and may present other causes of cognitive dysfunction.
Screening for depression, B12 deficiency, and hypothyroidism is recommended as these are treatable comorbidities commonly associated with MID.

Additional laboratory or radiologic testing is costly and has low yield, and thus is not recommended unless CNS syphilis is clinically suspected. See chapter on Dementia (Alzheimer's) for more on diagnostic evaluation for that condition.
If dementia is suspected, the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) and Mini-COG are useful screening tools.

In the Mini-COG, patients are asked to repeat three unrelated words, then draw a clock, then repeat the three words. If they are unable to repeat any words or if they repeat 1 or 2 but do not draw the clock correctly, dementia should be suspected.

The Brief Memory and Executive Test was more sensitive and specific than the MMSE for distinguishing MID from Alzheimer's dementia in persons with cognitive impairment, though it requires prospective validation, and the clinical utility is unclear.
A patient exhibiting cognitive decline without an apparently reversible cause should be evaluated for dementia, either with the MMSE, Mini-COG, or some other appropriate brief tool.

Patients who have vascular risk factors, recent stroke, or focal neurological findings should receive a brain MRI with and without contrast as well as a B12 level, thyroid-stimulating hormone, and depression screen.
Neuroradiologic or physical exam findings consistent with cerebrovascular disease are suggestive of MID in a demented patient.

The cholinesterase inhibitors donepezil, galantamine, and rivastigmine may offer some benefit for cognitive function and ADLs in patients with MID, so long as they tolerate the gastrointestinal side effects. It is uncertain whether benefits are clinically significant. B
Antipsychotic medications for behavioral disturbances should only be used after nonpharmacologic therapies have been attempted and if the benefits appear to outweigh the risks. C
Nonpharmacologic measures shown to be effective include massage therapy, cognitive training, graded assistance, and caregiver intervention. B
Modest benefits on cognition and ADLs have been shown in MID patients taking the cholinesterase inhibitors donepezil, galantamine, and rivastigmine, but their efficacy has not been compared.

For donepezil, NNT for 24 weeks was 23 to achieve modest improvement in objective cognitive scores.Because of cost and gastrointestinal side effects of the cholinesterase inhibitors, treatment should be individualized and based on a risk-benefit assessment. The NNH or cause an adverse event more than 24 weeks of treatment was 3 for donepezil compared to 6 for placebo.
Antipsychotic medicines are recommended for the treatment of psychosis and agitation only after exhausting nonpharmacologic approaches and after a risk-benefit assessment.

Aggressive control of vascular risk with antihypertensives, statins, and aspirin are generally recommended in patients with MID, as these agents have been shown to decrease risk for CVA. However, no study currently illustrates any measurable benefit of such measures in terms of cognitive function or ADLs in patients with MID.
The calcium channel blocker nimodipine may be effective for treatment of vascular dementia based on a systematic review.
There is no good data regarding aspirin for treatment of vascular dementia.

A trial randomized residents of long-term care facilities with moderate to severe dementia to gradually discontinue their anti-hypertensive medications or continue them. The study was stopped at 32 weeks because the intervention group (discontinuation) had no cognitive benefit and more adverse events.

A meta-analysis of 53 studies with 25,399 participants concluded that adults with neurocognitive disorders who take cholinesterase inhibitors are less likely to have falls (NNT = 102) but more likely to experience syncope than adults who take placebo (NNTH = 142).

A network meta-analysis identified 59 RCTs with 15,781 participants evaluating 15 different drugs for neuropsychiatric symptoms such as agitation. They concluded that risperidone has the best balance of effectiveness and adverse effects.
Hand massage may reduce agitated behavior, and light touch may improve ability to perform ADLs such as eating.
Bright light therapy minimally reduces cognitive decline, but does not decrease transfer rate to nursing home or mortality.
Decreased agitation and behavioral disturbance have been demonstrated with music during meals, bathing, and light exercise.
The Yizhi capsule and Zhiling decoction are Chinese herbal medicines for vascular dementia, but there are no RCTs of adequate quality to guide therapy.
Aromatherapy is not effective.
Aerobic physical exercise modestly improves attention and delayed memory function in demented patients.
Graded assistance, practice, and positive reinforcement may increase functional independence in demented patients.
Caregiver intervention programs have been shown to improve overall well-being of both patient and caregiver.
Cognitive training may slow functional decline in ability to perform ADLs.

A registry study grouped the HbA1c values of patients with T2DM and no dementia into 6 groups (< 6%; 6% to < 7%; 7% to < 8%; 8% to < 9%; 9% to < 10%; 10% or more). Among the cohort, the researchers had more than 4.6 million HbA1c measurements and a median 5.9 years of follow-up. Only persons with A1C persistently greater than 9.0% had an increased risk for dementia.
Many patients with MID, as with all forms of dementia, will eventually need a long-term care facility, and it is important that such facilities are well versed in caring for demented patients.
MID is irreversible; usual course is a continued stepwise deterioration marked by abrupt declines in cognitive function and increases in behavioral disturbances. C
Median survival beyond a diagnosis of all types of dementia is approximately 4.1 years for men and 4.6 years for women. B
